subject.title: Irvine — Measure D (Measure Directing the Use of Ranked Choice Voting for City Council Member and Mayoral Elections after January 1, 2028)

text: Shall a measure that directs, to the extent technically and financially feasible, the use of ranked choice voting for City Council Member and Mayoral Elections occurring after January 1, 2028, be adopted?
A “Yes” vote is in favor of adopting the measure and transitioning to RCV elections after January 1, 2028, if the specified technical and financial conditions are met.
A “No” vote is against adopting the measure.

analysis.title: Impartial Analysis

text: The City Council of the City of Irvine has placed a measure before the voters that would amend the Irvine Municipal Code to use ranked choice voting (RCV) for City Council member and mayoral elections after January 1, 2028, if certain technical and financial conditions are satisfied.

The City of Irvine (City) currently uses a plurality voting system for City Council member and mayoral elections. Under that system, voters vote for only one candidate and the person receiving the most votes wins the election even if they do not receive a majority of the votes.

In RCV elections, voters rank their choices in order of preference, such as first, second, third, and so on. If no candidate wins a majority of first-place votes, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated, and ballots ranking that candidate are transferred to the next-ranked continuing candidate. This process repeats until one candidate secures a majority of the votes counted in that round.
Under the proposed measure, the City would transition to RCV after January 1, 2028, once all of the following conditions are satisfied:
The available voting equipment can feasibly accommodate RCV;
Transitioning to RCV will not prevent the consolidation of City elections with elections conducted by the County of Orange; and

The additional cost for an RCV election is not more than 0.23% of the City’s general fund budget for the fiscal year during which the proposed RCV election would be held (RCV Cost Cap). For reference, 0.23% of the City’s fiscal year 2026-2027 general fund budget of approximately $312.1 million is approximately $717,790. However, the actual RCV Cost Cap would be calculated using the general fund budget for the fiscal year in which the proposed RCV election would be held. When the above conditions are met and the City transitions to RCV, the City will continue to conduct elections by RCV at every City Council member and mayoral election unless the voters choose another voting system. The proposed measure requires that RCV ballots allow the ranking of a minimum of five candidates, that write-in candidates be permitted, and that voters receive specific instructions regarding RCV. The proposed measure also establishes procedures for tabulating votes, resolving ties, resolving voting mistakes (e.g., skipping a ranking, or giving the same ranking to more than one candidate), conducting a manual vote tally, and providing reports for public review. The proposed measure authorizes the City Clerk to change those procedures if (1) the voting equipment will not feasibly accommodate the voting procedures, or (2) the Secretary of State changes its current RCV guidelines and adopts new guidelines that can be accommodated by the voting equipment.

strong: Vote YES on Measure D to Bring Fairer Elections to Irvine

text: Shouldn’t “majority rule” govern our elections? Yet in Irvine, candidates are regularly elected with less than one-third of the vote. Which means two-thirds of voters are represented by someone they don’t want. That is NOT real democracy.

RCV acts as an “instant runoff.” Voters rank their favorite candidates in order of preference: 1, 2, 3, and so on. If no candidate receives over 50% of first-choice rankings, the last-place candidate is eliminated, and their votes transfer to each voter’s second choice. This continues until a candidate wins a majority.

Never again will you have to vote for the “lesser evil.” RCV allows you to vote for your favorite candidate first, knowing your vote will still count toward your backup choice if your first choice loses.

Because candidates often need second and third choice rankings to win, negative campaigning backfires. Instead, RCV incentivizes positive, issue-oriented campaigns that unite rather than divide the community.

This measure ensures fiscal accountability with a strict safeguard: RCV will only be implemented if the cost is below 0.23% of the city’s budget. This responsibly modernizes our democracy while protecting your tax dollars.

Irvine deserves a democracy where the majority rules, candidates focus on solutions rather than negative attacks, and voters don’t have to settle for the “lesser evil.” Measure D delivers exactly that. Join dozens of cities in California and across the US using RCV.

And the only cost estimates come from the group pushing you to vote yes. Irvine can’t afford that kind of surprise: the city faces a $6 million deficit this year and a $47 million shortfall ahead.

strong: NO OTHER CITY IN ORANGE COUNTY USES THIS TODAY.

text: The Orange County Registrar admits in writing that it has no certified system for implementing ranked-choice voting — that’s why no infrastructure exists, and Irvine would bear the massive startup costs.
Irvine has never held a runoff election. This “fix” solves a problem we don’t have.

strong: “DOZENS OF CITIES”? LOOK WHAT HAPPENED THERE.

text: Implementation problems have surfaced across the country — including in Oakland, one of the flagship cities RCV advocates point to as proof it works. In 2022, a misconfigured algorithm led Alameda County to certify the wrong winner in an Oakland school board race. The certified winner was declared the loser weeks later, once the error was corrected. New York’s 2021 mayoral primary saw the same kind of chaos, when 135,000 test ballots were mistakenly counted.

strong: NO ONE KNOWS WHAT THIS WILL COST.

text: The Orange County Registrar of Voters has confirmed he does not have a state-certified system capable of running a ranked-choice election. He cannot say what it would cost or how long. The city’s estimates came not from the Registrar — but from ranked-choice voting advocacy groups. Those estimates already top $750,000 — before voter education, before county system upgrades, before anything goes wrong.
Cities that adopted ranked-choice voting did so to eliminate expensive runoff elections.
We don’t have the problem this is supposed to solve.
